title: How did you prepare these Qualification Rules?
answer:
Built on the foundation of WRTC 2026 and previous rules, this framework aims to provide a
consistent model for future organizers. Necessary adjustments—driven by community
feedback—were made to qualification events, geographic areas, score calculations, and penalty
guidelines for rule violations.

title: Why is the WRTC qualification contest list almost the same as for WRTC 2026?
answer:
We believe standardizing qualification events makes the process easier for participants by
eliminating the confusion of frequently changing criteria. Our objective is to maintain a stable list
of 12 eligible contests: 11 standard international events used in previous WRTCs, plus one contest
selected by the host country. For WRTC 2030, we have added the 9A DX Contest. Its mixed
CW/SSB format mirrors the WRTC structure and has gained steady popularity in recent years.

title: What about contests with no separate Assisted / Unassisted categories?
answer:
Following the precedent set by WRTC 2026, for contests that do not differentiate between
Assisted and Unassisted entries (such as CQ WPX), a weighting factor of 1.0 is applied to High
Power (HP) entrants, while a factor of 0.90 is applied to Low Power (LP) entrants

title: Why have you chosen these qualifying events?
answer:
▪ Event Selection: Winning any of these contests requires exceptional skill and persistence.
Based on past event analysis, this list represents a balanced, globally supported mix of
international DX contests ideal for identifying the world's strongest teams.
▪ Shorter Qualification Period: Competing at a world-class level demands significant
commitments of time, energy, and resources. To ease this burden, we have shortened the
traditional qualification period. It will begin in December 2026 (with the 9A DX Contest)



Questions and Answers
and conclude in November 2028 (with the CQ WW CW). Out of 24 total qualifying events
during this window, each participant only needs to submit their 10 best scores.
▪ More Preparation Time: Ending the qualification phase in late 2028 provides crucial extra
time ahead of July 2030. This allows us to confirm Team Leaders and Team Mates as early
as possible, giving teams at least a full year to practice together, optimize their station
setups, and finalize travel arrangements.

title: What is the rationale behind the Contest Category Weightings?
answer:
To avoid disrupting competitors' established strategies and station designs, we have largely
maintained the weighting criteria used in previous WRTCs. We retained the IARU HF
Championship and Low Power (LP) weighting adjustments introduced for WRTC 2026. The
primary modification is raising the weighting of the 9A DX Contest (organized by the host country)
to a full 1.0 to encourage wider participation.
Additionally, we increased the point values for the ARRL DX, All Asia, and WAE DX contests, but
only for the host continent of each event. For example:
• WAE DX Contest: 900 points for European entrants (800 points for entrants outside
Europe).
• ARRL International DX Contest: 900 points for the top North American (W/VE) Single-Op
All-Band (SO AB) score.
• All Asia DX Contest: 900 points for the top Asian Single-Op All-Band (SO AB) winning score.

title: How were the Qualification Areas and the number of teams allocated to each QA determined?
answer:
Historically, Qualification Areas (QAs) and team allocations are adjusted based on a statistical
analysis of global contest participation. Because a country's geographic size does not necessarily
correlate with its number of active contesters, these allocations must remain data-driven. For
WRTC 2030, the WRTC OC decided to keep the QAs largely unchanged from WRTC 2026, as recent
statistical analysis shows that global participation trends have remained stable. If a significant



Questions and Answers
shift occurs in the future—such as a substantial increase in activity from a specific region—future
organizers can adjust the QAs accordingly. Compared to the 30 QAs used in 2026, WRTC 2030 will
feature 29 QAs, with North American areas 10 and 11 merged into a single QA. Sub-areas will be
utilized to compensate for propagation differences, and the number of allocated teams has been
increased from 2 to 3.
So, what exactly are QA Sub-Areas and how they help overcome propagation difference?
A Qualification Area (QA) Sub-Area is a geographically defined subdivision of a QA established to
improve fairness in WRTC qualification score comparisons.
Because some QAs cover large regions, competitors operating from different locations within the
same QA may experience significantly different propagation conditions—particularly regarding
access to major contest centers. These variations can substantially impact available QSOs and
multipliers, making raw score comparisons less reflective of individual operating skill.
To reduce these geographical disadvantages, designated QAs are divided into Sub-Areas. Within
each Sub-Area, competitors' scores are evaluated against the highest applicable scores achieved
by stations operating from that same Sub-Area, following the calculation rules defined in Section
4 of the This approach allows leading competitors in geographically distinct Sub-Areas to achieve the
same maximum applicable WRTC Event Score, even if their raw contest scores differ significantly.
WRTC 2030 defines 13 standard score-comparison Sub-Areas across six QAs: EU #1, NA #1, NA
#6, NA #10, AF #1, and SA #2. An additional contest-specific comparison arrangement applies to
NA #10 for the ARRL DX Contest, as specified in Table 4 of the Sub-Areas are used solely for Event Score comparison and normalization. They do not constitute
independent QAs and do not increase the number of allocated team positions.
All competitors within the parent QA continue competing for its allocated Team Leader positions
based on their final Qualification Scores.
Ultimately, this mechanism minimizes the influence of geographical propagation advantages
while preserving a competitive qualification process focused on operator skill and performance.

title: How did you determine the number of qualifying and Special Teams?
answer:
The WRTC OC plans to expand the event to 60 competing teams, up from the 50-team baseline
used in WRTC 2026. To balance competitive integrity with financial and logistical realities, the 10
additional slots have been distributed as follows:
• Qualifying Teams (50 total, an increase of 8): We applied the largest increase to standard
qualifying slots, as standard qualification remains the core focus of the event. Based on
an analysis of logs from 2022–2025 contests and the overall increase in WRTC teams, the
8 extra slots have been allocated as follows: Europe (+5), North America (+2), and Africa
(+1).
• Defending Champions (1 total, unchanged): Reserved for the winners of WRTC 2026.
• Sponsored Teams (4 total, an increase of 2): Expanding the event to 60 teams introduces
significant logistical costs. Adding two sponsored slots provides a financial safety net to
ensure the larger event is securely funded.
• Youth Teams (3 total) & Wild Card Teams (2 total): We shifted one slot from the Youth
category to the Wild Card category. While we strongly encourage high-level competitors
under 25, we cannot guarantee enough highly competitive youth entries to lock in four
dedicated slots years in advance. Adding a Wild Card maintains flexibility: if there is a surge
of exceptional youth scores, the OC can use it to invite a fourth youth team.

title: At a glance, many of the rules are the same as for previous WRTCs. What changes would you highlight or summarize?
answer:
Summary of Significant Changes for WRTC 2030 Qualification
General Rule Updates
• Transparency & Fair Play: An increased focus on promoting fair competition both during
the qualification period and at the WRTC event itself.
• Disqualification Penalties: We have aligned WRTC penalties with standard contest
practices. Because most qualifying contests bar disqualified (DQ) stations from receiving
awards the following year, WRTC 2030 will apply a similar standard for eligibility.



Questions and Answers
• Long-Term Standardization: We intentionally kept rules, qualification events,
Qualification Areas (QAs), and technical setups as stable as possible. Minimizing changes
makes it much easier for global competitors to develop and execute a multi-year
qualification strategy.
Youth TL Changes
• Separate & Visible Interim Standings: To keep young operators motivated and engaged
throughout the entire cycle, qualification standings for youth participants will be tracked
separately. Youth competitors are responsible for indicating this in their log submissions
by entering their personal callsign followed by (Youth) in brackets (e.g., Operator IZ7XYZ
(Youth)).
• Reduced Qualifying Events: Because many youth participants lack access to competitive
home stations, they may operate from other locations as guests or multi-operator team
members. To ease travel requirements, the required number of qualifying events for Youth
TLs is reduced from 10 to 6 (with a maximum of 2 multi-operator entries). Scores are
calculated according to the operating QA; for instance, if a participant's home QA is NA#01
and they submit up to 4 out-of-home QA scores, each event score is measured against the
best category score in that specific QA. Final selection is determined by the highest overall
youth scores worldwide.
• Relaxed Out-of-Area Restrictions: To broaden opportunities for students or those relying
on remote stations, youth operators may compete from outside their regular Home
Qualification Area. Out of the 6 total event scores, a maximum of 4 may be outside-QA
entries (operated either remotely or on-site).
Scoring & Weighting Updates
• ARRL Int’l DX, All Asia, and WAE DX Contests: Point values have been increased to 900
points for designated primary region stations. This adjustment applies exclusively to the
organizer's continent participants: W/VE stations for ARRL, Asian stations for All Asia, and



Questions and Answers
European stations (per the WAE country list) for WAE. While this does not affect DX
entrants, it acknowledges the efforts and activity of the host region.
• 9A DX Contest Added (1000 points): The host country's contest, featuring a worldwide
format similar to IARU-WRTC rules, has been added to the baseline list to encourage wider
participation.
• Assisted & Unassisted Weightings Equalized: Single Operator (SO) Assisted and
Unassisted weighting factors have been adjusted to be equal, recognizing that both
categories demand specific, highly challenging skill sets.
• Low Power (LP) Weighting Reduced: While we fully agree that LP operating requires
exceptional skill (e.g., holding a run frequency, breaking pileups, and advanced operating
strategy), power limit violations (exceeding 100W) remain a widespread issue. Until
contest organizers can more effectively penalize these violations, maintaining a high
weighting factor for LP risks inadvertently rewarding rule-breakers rather than legitimate
skill.
Changes in Qualification Areas and Teams
WRTC 2026 Qualification Areas were followed as closely as possible to ensure the fairest possible
slot distribution. Only limited changes were made, primarily to reflect the increase in
geographically qualifying teams from 42 to 50, alongside insights from log and score analyses
from 2022–2025.
The QAs and team allocations were prepared in accordance with the WRTC SC’s
recommendations regarding structure and distribution. We also defined three operational
scenarios regarding when and under what conditions claiming scores from outside a Home Area
is permitted:
1. Home QA Operations
2. Outside QA Operations (maximum of 3)
3. Alternate Home QA (for ongoing connections and contest activity conducted from a QA
different from the Home QA).

title: Given that four teams were disqualified at WRTC 2026, is the WRTC OC implementing additional measures to prevent cheating?
answer:
The WRTC 2030 OC is fully committed to ensuring the fairest possible qualification process, and
we expect the support of both qualifying contest organizers and the global contesting community
in this effort. Our primary goal is to significantly reduce opportunities for cheating during the
qualification period and foster a culture of integrity. Because radiosport relies heavily on personal



Questions and Answers
honesty, future organizers—working closely with the WRTC SC and WRTC JC—will prioritize this
issue by implementing clear, strict rules and decisive penalties for any violations.
Exceptions for Team Leaders (TL) with Marginal Scores:
• Applies to entrants from Qualification Areas with multiple DXCCs, where some may have
a limited number of contestants but qualify as a TL based on the DXCC TL maximum limit
of other QA DXCC entrants, with substantially more competitive WRTC score.
• Their scores may be compared against scores from DXCC that already reached TL quota.
• If there are substantially higher, competitive scores near the threshold of a capped DXCC
entity, the WRTC OC may grant an exception based on a review of the circumstances.
